listenings.text: Right, let us get started. Before we go over the numbers, I want to bring up something from last week. Two of you reached out to me about the March deadline, and I would rather deal with it now than have it come up at the end. So: I am going to point out one thing and then I will hand over to Adriana. The thing I want to point out is that nobody has signed off on the global rollout, and I have heard three people this week talk as if somebody had. If you want to push back on the date, push back today. If we cannot narrow it down to one date in this meeting, we will circle back on Thursday, and Thursday is the last time we look at this.

Adriana, one piece of advice about the way you write and the way you speak, because they are not the same and both of them are correct. In the meeting, say bring up, go over, push back, circle back. That is what the room says, and using the formal word out loud can make you sound distant. But when you write the minutes, or the policy, or anything that a lawyer might read, use the single word: raise, review, object, revisit. There is one rule you have to respect either way. If you use a pronoun with a separable phrasal verb, the pronoun goes in the middle. You bring it up. You never bring up it. That one is not a matter of style.
